info.title: Hunger and Concentration in Daily Life: Inter-Individual Differences and Eating-Related Variation but No Robust Average Association

text.text: Momentary reductions in concentration may affect daily functioning.
In addition to external distractors, bodily signals might divert attention from ongoing tasks.
Hunger might not only signal short dips in energy supply but also trigger distracting interoceptive sensations.
We focus on hunger as a frequent sensation that is regularly regulated through food intake and therefore may display a complex relation to concentration.
To test the relation between hunger and concentration, 63 participants in an experience sampling study reported their momentary concentration, hunger, and food intake six times daily for four weeks.
Using Bayesian multilevel within between models, we assessed the hunger concentration association and, in exploratory analyses, whether this relation differed depending on prior food intake.
We found no robust average hunger concentration association, with a Bayes Factor supporting the absence of a systematic population-level within-participant association.
At the same time, the association varied considerably between individuals.
The association did not differ depending on prior food intake overall.
In exploratory meal-specific-analyses, more negative hunger concentration associations were estimated after breakfast and lunch compared with assessments without the respective meal.
Thus, the momentary hunger concentration relation in daily life was characterised by considerable inter-individual differences and possible differences by specific meal contexts.
These findings suggest that everyday concentration may be shaped less by hunger per se than by individual differences and the context in which hunger occurs.
Many daily tasks and decisions require focused attention or concentration.
Simultaneously, distractions constantly threaten our focus or direct it elsewhere.
Concentration fluctuates in daily life and is influenced by multiple internal and external factors.
Broadly, these influences can be distinguished into bottom-up factors, such as fatigue or hunger, and top-down factors, such as intentions and motivations (Hagger, 2016).
text.formatted: Broadly, these influences can be distinguished into bottom-up factors, such as fatigue or hunger, and top-down factors, such as intentions and motivations <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Hagger, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In this sense, concentration can be understood as the capacity to maintain focus on ongoing thoughts or actions despite competing bottom-up signals.
When such bottom-up signals become salient, they may interfere with concentration and thereby make it harder to pursue intended goals.
For example, feeling hungry may distract us from working on a task that we deem personally important.
Identifying momentary reductions in concentration due to such bottomup challenges therefore helps to understand when and why individuals struggle to stay focused in daily life.
Hunger is an important bottom-up bodily signal with a complex aetiology.

Perceived hunger is related to glucose levels (Jin et al., 2026; Wyatt et al., 2021), stomach distension resulting from food intake (Maljaars et al., 2007) and insulin-and ghrelin-levels (Flint et al.,  2007).
text.formatted: Perceived hunger is related to glucose levels <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Jin et al., 2026;</ref> Wyatt et al., 2021), stomach distension resulting from food intake <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Maljaars et al., 2007) and</ref> insulin-and ghrelin-levels (Flint et al.,  2007).

text.text: However, subjective hunger is also shaped by non-physiological factors like learned associations, and contextual influences.
That is, hunger may partly arise as a conditioned anticipatory response to cues previously associated with eating.
For example, a school bell signalling lunch break may, through repeated pairing with food intake, elicit hunger sensations (Stevenson et al., 2024).
text.formatted: For example, a school bell signalling lunch break may, through repeated pairing with food intake, elicit hunger sensations <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Stevenson et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, situational factors like seeing others eat can also affect hunger momentarily (Herman, 2015).
text.formatted: Finally, situational factors like seeing others eat can also affect hunger momentarily <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Herman, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Adding to this complexity, food intake regulates hunger and thereby changes the context in which hunger is experienced.
This multi-layered aetiology implies that hunger sensation differs between individuals due to differences in physiology and learning experience, and between moments due to different contexts.
Concentration requires energy.
Thus, it can be hypothesised that higher hunger, as a correlate of a transient reduction in available energy, may be related to a reduced capacity for concentration.
Additionally, hunger-related thoughts may also compete with task-focused concentration.
Considering the multifaceted aetiology of hunger, the hunger-concentration association may vary between individuals with different life histories and varying contexts.
Previous research indicates that hungry moments may indeed be moments of lower concentration.
Hunger may increase mind-wandering (Rummel & Nied, 2017).

text.text: We conducted a four-week experience sampling study with six daily measurements, distinguishing momentary within participant deviations in hunger from between participant differences.

text.text: In an exploratory analysis that was not preregistered, we tested whether the hunger concentration relation differed depending on prior food intake.
The study protocol is also described in detail in a previous publication (Bamberg et al., 2026).

text.text: This experience sampling study was conducted entirely remotely.
First, participants answered trait and demographics questionnaires.
They were then instructed during a video call on how to use the m-Path app (Mestdagh et al., 2023) for responding to the questions, and experimenters explained each question.

text.text: Participants responded to the same questions six times daily for four weeks at fixed time windows using a signal-contingent sampling scheme.
Prompts were sent at 08:30 AM, 11:00 AM, 01:30 PM, 04:00 PM, 06:30 PM, 09:30 PM.
The first questionnaire was available between 08:30 AM and 10:00 AM, the last between 09:30 PM and 12:00 AM each day.
For the remaining four prompts, participants were able to open the questionnaire within 60 minutes.
To ensure data quality, only participants with a response rate above 50% for all prompts were included in the analysis.
We recruited a convenience sample of participants via social media, flyers distributed on university campus and in the city and a university psychology participant pool.
Enrolment ran from January to May 2025.
Inclusion criteria were age 18 60 years, BMI 18.5 30 kg/m^2, no current or past eating disorder.
We restricted the BMI range to reduce heterogeneity in hunger and satiety processes associated with more extreme weight status.
Together with the eating disorder exclusion criterion, this also reduced potential burden associated with repeated assessments of hunger and eating.

The required sample size was calculated for another research question and the present analysis should therefore be considered a secondary analysis that was not specifically powered for the hunger and concentration association.
Out of 71 enrolled participants, data from 8 were excluded due to a low response rate and premature termination, leaving 63 participants for the analysis.
Participants were mostly female (f = 50 (78%), m = 12 (19%), d = 1 (2%)), in their midtwenties (M = 25.24 years, SD = 8.15) and university students (N = 53; employed N = 9; unemployed = 1).

In our daily life study, subjective hunger was not robustly associated with subjective concentration on average.
Yet, the association varied considerably between individuals, suggesting that the hunger concentration relation is not uniform across individuals.
Our findings therefore do not support a general negative association between hunger and concentration.
Instead, individual characteristics in physiology, perception, and appetitive learning history may contribute to differences in how hunger relates to concentration.
Furthermore, we explored whether the hunger concentration relation differed when individuals had eaten or not.

While the association was not different when considering food-intake at any time of the day, exploratory analyses suggested more negative hunger concentration associations after breakfast and lunch compared with the corresponding assessments without these meals.
These exploratory findings should be interpreted cautiously but may indicate interesting times of the day to consider in future research.
A possible reason why we did not observe a robust overall hunger concentration relation is that participants ate at relatively short intervals throughout the day.
Food intake typically started with breakfast in the morning and extended to after-dinner snacks at night, often shortly before sleep.
On average, participants ate every two and a half hours, mirroring earlier findings from a US sample (Gill & Panda, 2015).
text.formatted: On average, participants ate every two and a half hours, mirroring earlier findings from a US sample <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Gill & Panda, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with this frequent food intake, hunger was relatively low on average, although there was considerable variation in reported hunger.
This may explain why subjective hunger was not very informative for concentration overall and limits the situations to which our findings can be generalized.
Notwithstanding, the exploratory eating specific analyses suggested that meal context may matter in specific situations.
Meal intake may resolve hunger and therefore eliminate a momentary distractor of concentration.
Conversely, large meals can induce tiredness due to the autonomic nervous system prioritising digestion (Reyner et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Conversely, large meals can induce tiredness due to the autonomic nervous system prioritising digestion <ref type="bibr">(Reyner et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, highfat, large lunches transiently reduced cognitive performance according to a systematic review of 11 studies (Müller et al., 2013).
text.formatted: For instance, highfat, large lunches transiently reduced cognitive performance according to a systematic review of 11 studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Müller et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: These processes suggest that the relation between hunger and concentration may be different depending on whether food was recently consumed.
In the exploratory analysis, more negative hunger concentration associations were estimated after breakfast and lunch compared with assessments where the respective meal had not been consumed.
In contrast, there was no clear interaction for afternoon snack intake.
This pattern may indicate that the meaning or consequences of hunger differ depending on the preceding meal context.
In related research on time-restricted eating and intermittent fasting, selfreported concentration increased after participants had broken the fast (Bamberg, Reichenberger, et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In related research on time-restricted eating and intermittent fasting, selfreported concentration increased after participants had broken the fast <ref type="bibr">(Bamberg, Reichenberger, et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: While this finding does not directly support a moderation effect, it illustrates that subjective concentration may be related to eating context.
Our findings extend this perspective by suggesting that not only concentration itself, but also its association with hunger, may differ depending on prior food intake.
However, these analyses were not preregistered, involved several comparisons, and should be considered hypothesisgenerating.
We suggest the following testable hypothesis: higher post-prandial hunger is associated with lower subjective concentration than hunger without previous food-intake, especially for breakfast.
One possible interpretation is that hunger after a meal carries a different meaning than hunger before eating.
Before eating, hunger may be anticipated and therefore less disruptive.
After eating, however, continued or renewed hunger may violate expectations of satiety.
Such unexpected hunger may be more salient and therefore more strongly related to lower concentration.
This interpretation is consistent with evidence that expectations can shape responses to food intake.

For example, expected portion size can influence cephalic phase responses independent of actual portion size (Crum et al., 2011), and expected effects of hunger can affect cognitive performance independent of actual satiety levels (Bamberg & Roefs, 2025).
text.formatted: For example, expected portion size can influence cephalic phase responses independent of actual portion size <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Crum et al., 2011)</ref>, and expected effects of hunger can affect cognitive performance independent of actual satiety levels <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bamberg & Roefs, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: A second, not mutually exclusive explanation is that hunger after eating reflected insufficient satiety or postprandial physiological dynamics.

Glucose dips two to three hours after breakfast have been associated with subjective hunger in an ambulatory assessment study, whereas the immediate rise in blood glucose after consumption showed no such relation (Wyatt et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Glucose dips two to three hours after breakfast have been associated with subjective hunger in an ambulatory assessment study, whereas the immediate rise in blood glucose after consumption showed no such relation <ref type="bibr">(Wyatt et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This provides one possible explanation for the breakfast pattern, although we did not measure glucose and therefore cannot test this mechanism directly.

Future studies should therefore assess breakfast composition, satiety expectations, perceived energy requirements, and physiological markers such as continuous glucose more directly to clarify the link between breakfast, hunger, and concentration.
It is also possible that concentration was particularly salient during the morning, when participants may have been engaged in cognitively demanding work or study activities.
However, the similar pattern observed for lunch suggests that this explanation is unlikely to account for the meal specific findings alone.

text.text: Furthermore, continuous blood-glucose monitors could deliver important information on the physiological side of hunger.
Several limitations of this research should be mentioned.
First, hunger was relatively low on average in our sample, consistent with the frequent food intake observed throughout the day.
This restricted range of hunger may have reduced our ability to observe a robust hunger concentration association and limits the situations to which our findings can be generalised.
At the same time, this eating pattern likely reflects common behaviour in the sampled population and is therefore informative of hunger and concentration under everyday conditions.
In addition, the sample consisted predominantly of young women and university students.
Participants with BMI below 18.5 or above 30 kg/m² and individuals with a history of eating disorders were excluded.

We excluded these groups since interoception differs between obese as well as disordered eaters and normal-weight individuals, which could affect the sensation of hunger and its influence on concentration (Martin et al., 2019; Robinson et al., 2021).
text.formatted: We excluded these groups since interoception differs between obese as well as disordered eaters and normal-weight individuals, which could affect the sensation of hunger and its influence on concentration <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Martin et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Robinson et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The findings therefore generalise most directly to young adults within this BMI range and should not be assumed to apply equally to older populations or individuals with more extreme BMI or eating disorder histories.
Second, eating behaviour, metabolic interoception, and cognition are complex phenomena.
Short momentary questions may not fully capture how participants understand hunger or concentration in specific contexts.
By modelling differences between individuals, we could account for some of this heterogeneity.
Still, incorporating more individualised or context-sensitive assessments may better reflect the way these constructs are experienced in daily life.
Relatedly, our design does not allow strong conclusions about directionality.
Hunger may influence concentration, but lower concentration may also change how hunger is noticed or reported, or both may be shaped by other momentary factors.
Future work should therefore investigate these relations with designs that better address temporal ordering or with experimental studies.
A further limitation concerns the bimodal distribution of concentration.
The response format may have contributed to this pattern because the slider was initialised at its midpoint and participants were required to move it before submitting a response.
Initialising sliders at the midpoint can itself induce multimodality in intensive longitudinal data (Haslbeck et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Initialising sliders at the midpoint can itself induce multimodality in intensive longitudinal data <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Haslbeck et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, the bimodality may not be solely a measurement artefact.
It could also indicate that participants experienced or reported concentration in more discrete states rather than as a continuously varying construct.
Importantly, the Gaussian model did not reproduce this bimodal distribution in the posterior predictive check (Figure S1), although it approximated the overall variability in concentration.
text.formatted: Importantly, the Gaussian model did not reproduce this bimodal distribution in the posterior predictive check (Figure <ref type="figure">S1</ref>), although it approximated the overall variability in concentration.

text.text: We retained the Gaussian likelihood to estimate average associations, but acknowledge that it does not fully represent the distribution of the outcome.
Future studies should carefully consider initialising sliders at the midpoint and could compare continuous ratings with response formats that allow more discrete concentration states.

A simpler response format, for example single-choice items J Op-E ]"4σJ] p -OpE p 84pO 8"]σ cp '4 pO 8"]σ cpE8[p OJ"OpO 8"]σ cp-E pbe a worthwhile measurement alternative of these concepts in future experience sampling studies.
Finally, the sample size was determined for another research question and the present secondary analysis was therefore not specifically powered for the hunger concentration association.
Replication in an independent sample is particularly important for the exploratory eating specific findings.

Furthermore, differences in hunger distributions between eating conditions and potential non-linearity in the hunger concentration association cannot be fully ruled out as alternative explanations for the exploratory interactions.
Overall, subjective hunger was not robustly related to subjective concentration in daily life, but the relation varied across individuals and may depend on recent meal context.
The exploratory meal specific findings require replication.

Notwithstanding, these findings suggest that understanding hunger concentration relations in everyday life will require more individualised and context sensitive assessment rather than assuming a uniform effect of hunger.
